summary.text: Weather forecasting applies science and technology to predict what the atmosphere will be like at a given place and time.
Forecasters collect data on the current atmosphere, land and ocean and now rely on computer models, though people still pick which model to base a forecast on.
Because the atmosphere is chaotic and starting measurements carry errors, forecasts get less accurate the further ahead they reach.

items.prompt: In 2009 the US spent about $5.8 billion on weather forecasting. Roughly how large were the estimated benefits?

options.label: About half of what was spent
About the same as what was spent
About six times what was spent
About sixty times what was spent

items.explain: The benefits were estimated at six times the roughly $5.8 billion spent.

items.prompt: You compare tomorrow's outlook with one for ten days from now. Which deserves more trust?

options.label: Tomorrow's, since accuracy drops with range
The ten-day one, since it uses more data
Both equally, since one model makes both
Neither, since forecasts are pure guesses

items.explain: Forecasts become less accurate as the gap between now and the forecast time grows.

items.prompt: What invention began the modern age of weather forecasting in the 1830s?

options.label: The weather satellite
The electric telegraph
The electronic computer
The weather balloon

items.explain: The electric telegraph let reports from a wide area arrive almost instantly, so forecasters could use conditions further upwind.

items.prompt: A forecast centre runs many versions of a forecast, and most of them agree on rain Saturday. What does that agreement give the forecaster?

options.label: A guarantee that it will rain
A reason to skip new observations
Proof that the atmosphere is not chaotic
A narrower error and more confidence

items.explain: Using ensembles and model consensus helps narrow the error and gives confidence in the forecast.

items.prompt: An old saying claims a red sunset means fair weather the next day. How have rules like this held up?

options.label: Every one has been proven reliable
They only ever worked at sea
Many fail rigorous statistical testing
Computers have confirmed them all

items.explain: Weather lore came from patterns noticed over generations, but many of its predictions do not stand up to rigorous statistical testing.

items.prompt: Computers now do the heavy calculations. What job still needs a person?

options.label: Solving the equations on paper
Picking the best model to trust
Measuring every input by hand
Turning the numbers into code

items.explain: Human input is still needed to choose the best model, drawing on pattern recognition and knowledge of how models perform and where they are biased.
